title: Chapter 56 — Of the Less Erroneous Pictures of Whales, and the True
paragraphs: In connection with the monstrous pictures of whales, I am strongly tempted here to take up those still more monstrous stories about them which are found in certain books, both ancient and modern, especially in Pliny, Purchas, Hackluyt, Harris, Cuvier, and so forth. But I will let that matter pass.

I know of only four published outlines of the great Sperm Whale: Colnett's, Huggins's, Frederick Cuvier's, and Beale's. In the previous chapter Colnett and Cuvier were referred to. Huggins's is far better than theirs; but Beale's is by far the best. All of Beale's drawings of this whale are good, except the middle figure in the picture of three whales in various attitudes that heads his second chapter. His frontispiece, boats attacking Sperm Whales, though no doubt likely to provoke the polite skepticism of some parlor men, is admirably correct and lifelike in its general effect. Some of the Sperm Whale drawings in J. Ross Browne are pretty correct in outline; but they are wretchedly engraved. That is not his fault, though.

Of the Right Whale, the best outline pictures are in Scoresby. But they are drawn on too small a scale to give the impression one would want. He has only one picture of whaling scenes, and this is a sad deficiency, because it is only through such pictures, when done even reasonably well, that you can get anything like a truthful idea of the living whale as seen by his living hunters.

But all things considered, by far the finest pictures of whales and whaling scenes to be found anywhere, though not the most accurate in some details, are two large, well-made French engravings based on paintings by one Garnery. One shows an attack on the Sperm Whale, the other an attack on the Right Whale. In the first, a noble Sperm Whale appears in the full majesty of his power, just risen from the depths of the ocean beneath the boat and carrying high on his back the terrific wreckage of its smashed planks. The prow of the boat is partly intact and is drawn just balancing on the monster's spine; and standing in that prow, for one single flash of time too brief to measure, you see an oarsman, half hidden by the whale's furious, boiling spout, in the act of leaping as if from a cliff. The action of the whole scene is wonderfully good and true. The half-emptied line-tub floats on the whitened sea; the wooden shafts of the spilled harpoons bob slantwise in it; the heads of the swimming crew are scattered around the whale, their faces showing fright in contrasting ways; while in the black, stormy distance the ship is bearing down on the scene. You could find serious fault with the anatomical details of this whale, but let that go, since for the life of me I could not draw one as good.

In the second engraving, the boat is just drawing up beside the barnacled flank of a big Right Whale on the run, who rolls his black, weedy bulk through the sea like a mossy rockslide off the Patagonian cliffs. His jets stand straight up, full and black as soot, so that with so much smoke pouring from the chimney you would think a fine supper must be cooking in the great bowels below. Seabirds are pecking at the little crabs, shellfish, and other sea candies and macaroni that the Right Whale sometimes carries on his pestilent back. And all the while the thick-lipped leviathan is tearing through the deep, leaving tons of churning white curds in his wake and making the light boat rock in the swells like a skiff caught close to the paddle-wheels of an ocean steamer. So the foreground is all raging commotion; but behind it, in admirable artistic contrast, lies the glassy surface of a sea in a dead calm, the limp, unstarched sails of the helpless ship, and the inert mass of a dead whale — a conquered fortress — with the flag of capture hanging lazily from the whale-pole planted in his spout-hole.

Who Garnery the painter is, or was, I don't know. But I'd bet my life that he either knew his subject at first hand or was marvelously coached by some experienced whaleman. When it comes to painting action, the French are the lads. Go and look at all the paintings of Europe: where will you find such a gallery of living, breathing commotion on canvas as in that triumphal hall at Versailles, where the viewer fights his way pell-mell through one great battle of France after another; where every sword seems a flash of the Northern Lights, and armed kings and Emperors dash by one after another like a charge of crowned centaurs? These sea battle-pieces of Garnery are not wholly unworthy of a place in that gallery.

The natural French gift for catching the picturesque side of things seems especially evident in the paintings and engravings they have made of whaling scenes. With not a tenth of England's experience in the fishery, and not a thousandth of America's, they have still supplied both nations with the only finished sketches that can at all convey the real spirit of the whale hunt. English and American whale draftsmen mostly seem perfectly satisfied to give the mechanical outline of things, such as the whale's vacant profile — which, as far as picturesque effect goes, amounts to about the same as sketching the profile of a pyramid. Even Scoresby, the justly famous Right whaleman, after giving us a stiff full-length portrait of the Greenland whale and three or four delicate miniatures of narwhals and porpoises, treats us to a series of classic engravings of boat hooks, chopping knives, and grapnels; and with the microscopic diligence of a Leuwenhoeck (the pioneer of the microscope) he lays before a shivering world ninety-six facsimiles of magnified Arctic snow crystals. I mean no slight to the excellent voyager (I honor him as a veteran), but in so important a matter it was surely an oversight not to have gotten a sworn affidavit for every crystal, taken before a Greenland Justice of the Peace.

Besides those fine engravings after Garnery, there are two other French engravings worth noting, by someone who signs himself "H. Durand." One of them, though not exactly suited to our present purpose, still deserves mention for other reasons. It is a quiet noon scene among the islands of the Pacific: a French whaler anchored close inshore in a calm, lazily taking on water, the loosened sails of the ship and the long palm leaves behind her drooping together in the windless air. The effect is very fine, considering that it shows the hardy fishermen in one of their rare moments of oriental repose. The other engraving is a very different matter. The ship lies hove-to on the open sea, in the very heart of leviathan life, with a Right Whale alongside; the vessel (busy cutting-in) heels over toward the monster as if toward a wharf; and a boat, hastily pushing off from all this activity, is about to chase some whales in the distance. The harpoons and lances lie leveled and ready; three oarsmen are just stepping the mast into its hole; and a sudden roll of the sea has lifted the little craft half upright out of the water, like a rearing horse. From the ship, the smoke of the boiling whale's torments rises like the smoke over a village of smithies; and to windward, a black cloud rising with its promise of squalls and rain seems to spur on the excited seamen.
